This article preliminarily characterizes political fake news on Twitter using meta-data from more than 1.5M tweets collected on Donald Trump's election day, finding significant differences in followers, URLs, and user verification.
The paragraph contains ].

Fake news became mainstream in politics during the 2016 United States presidential election, prompting government and corporate efforts despite limited ability to define, identify, and stop its spread.

Since the Obama campaign in 2008, social media has been pervasive in United States politics, with up to 62% of American adults receiving news from social media and platforms facilitating fake news diffusion.

Craig Silverman confirmed the rise of fake news, stating that top-performing fake election news stories on Facebook generated more engagement than top stories from major news outlets in the final three months of the US presidential campaign.
The research assumes social media is a conduit for fake news and uses more that 1.5M tweets collected on November 8th 2016 to identify meta-data features of tweets containing fake news.

The goals are to compare fake-news and non-fake-news tweets, characterize viral fake-news tweets and originating accounts through meta-data, and determine political polarization in tweets containing fake news.
The study uses number of retweets to identify viral tweets, defines fake news using Rubin et al. BIBREF7 categories, and uses a manually labelled, publicly released dataset BIBREF8.
The paragraph states that main observations can be made from the results.

The findings resonate with Allcot and Gentzkow BIBREF9, provide external validity to previous research, and stress the importance of meta-data and useful parameters for identifying fake news on Twitter.
The rest of the paper discusses literature, hypotheses, data, methodology, findings, conclusions, and future lines of work.
A survey by Conroy and colleagues BIBREF10 identifies linguistic approaches and network approaches using network characteristics and meta-data to single-out fake news.
Psychology, political science, and sociology studies examine why people consume or believe misinformation, consistently reporting roles for priming effects and confirmation bias.
An Economics paper BIBREF9 found fake news sites often mimic legitimate organizations, are short-lived, are more likely shared than trusted-source articles, and exhibit larger polarization.
The work relies on Rubin et al. BIBREF7 categorization to describe fake news and introduces five categories with illustrative examples from the dataset.
Previous works suggest determinants for adoption and diffusion of fake news, and the hypotheses identify three dimensions that may distinguish fake news from legit information.
The proposed hypotheses concern features believed to identify tweets containing fake news from those not containing them and will be tested over the collected dataset.
The paragraph names Exposure.
The paragraph names Characterization.
The paragraph names Polarization.
Public tweets were collected via Twitter's public API using election-related hashtags and user handles on Nov 8th 2016, with data collection running for just one day.
The study characterizes viral tweets containing fake news, defines viral as retweeted more than 1000 times, and discusses retweet functionality and reasons for retweeting.
After creating the viral tweets dataset, duplicates were eliminated and an expert manually labelled tweet text as containing fake news or not, producing publicly available annotated dataset BIBREF8.
The study uses fields within tweets returned by Twitter's API to compare distributions between viral tweets containing fake news and viral tweets not containing fake news.

The next section graphically describes attribute distributions, normalizes or takes logarithms where appropriate, and uses the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test with the null hypothesis that both distributions are equal.
The sample contained 1 785 855 tweets from 848 196 users, including 1327 viral tweets from 643 users retweeted 290 841 times by the 8th of November 2016.
A single person annotated the 1327 viral tweets, identifying 136 as potentially containing fake news, while noting ambiguity and that the dataset is not claimed as ground truth.
The results detail tweet characteristics along previously mentioned dimensions, and Table TABREF23 reports differences and associated p-values for every variable considered.
Figure FIGREF24 shows viral tweets containing fake news were created more recently, exposing Twitter users to election-related fake news for a shorter period.
Figure FIGREF25 shows no apparent retweet difference, and the Kolmogorov-Smirnoff test does not discard the hypothesis that the associated distributions are equal.
Users generating at least a viral tweet containing fake news appear to have fewer favourites on average, but Figure FIGREF26 differences are not statistically significant.
Viral fake news appears to use more hashtags, but Figure FIGREF27 shows no statistical difference between average hashtags in viral tweets and viral fake news.

Of 82 users spreading fake news, 34 had verified accounts and 48 unverified, with 6 suspended, 3 imitating legitimate accounts, and 4 deleted; Figure FIGREF28 shows fake news more likely from unverified accounts.
Accounts distributing fake news appear to have the same average number of friends, but Figure FIGREF29 shows a statistically significant difference in friends distributions.

Accounts generating viral tweets with fake news have a very different follower distribution from those generating viral tweets with no fake news, with statistically significant differences in Figure FIGREF30.
Figures FIGREF31 and FIGREF32 show accounts spreading viral tweets with fake news have, on average, a larger friends/followers ratio, while non-fake-news accounts are more evenly distributed.
Figure FIGREF33 shows viral tweets labelled as containing fake news use mentions less frequently, mostly containing 1 mention versus two in other tweets, with statistically significant differences.
Figure FIGREF34 shows tweets labelled as not containing fake news appear to present more media elements than fake-news tweets, but the difference is not statistically significant.
Figure FIGREF35 shows viral tweets containing fake news include more URLs to other sites, with a statistically significant distribution difference assuming INLINEFORM0.

Manual inspection found 117 viral tweets labelled as containing fake news supported Donald Trump, 8 supported Hillary Clinton, and the remaining tweets concerned other topics without candidate support.
The paragraph introduces observations, constrained by the existing dataset, about differences between viral tweets labelled as containing fake news and viral tweets labelled as not containing them.

Findings related to Table TABREF44 suggest specific meta-data may identify fake news, especially time of exposure, shorter-lived viral fake-news tweets, deleted or suspended accounts, and scrutiny of newly created accounts.

Accounts spreading fake news have a larger friends/followers proportion and tweets containing fake news have more URLs, suggesting these features could single-out fake news and align with click-through advertising incentives.
Viral fake news content was highly polarized, aligning with Alcott et al. BIBREF9 and suggesting textual sentiment analysis plus meta-data parameters may help identify fake news.

The paper presents a preliminary study of meta-data from a publicly available dataset of tweets that became viral during the 2016 US presidential election day, aiming to understand features of viral fake-news tweets.
The authors argue automatic identification requires understanding and modelling deceitful tweets, anticipate spam-like evolution, and present a complementary angle to content-focused work.

Within the used dataset, differences around exposure, account characteristics, and content tone suggest fake news can be modelled and automatically detected, with plans to validate in an extended sample until 4 months after the US election.
No competing financial interest exist.
